lead: Both readings ask the same question: whom do you serve? Paul tells the Romans that every life is given to some master, either to sin, which pays its wages in death, or to God, whose gift is eternal life. In Mark, the disciples have been arguing about who is the greatest, and Jesus puts a child in their midst. Yesterday's evening Gospel brought us to the same house in Capernaum. The key words are slave, servant and child.

set: Paul has just proclaimed that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (5:20). Some drew a wrong conclusion: then let us go on sinning. Paul answers it twice in chapter 6. The first time he speaks of Baptism, in which we died with Christ to sin (6:1–14). The second time, in our passage, he uses the picture of slavery, which everyone in Rome understood, since a large part of the city's people were slaves or freed slaves.
str: v. 15: the question: shall we sin because we are under grace?
vv. 16–18: everyone is the slave of the one he obeys; you have passed from sin to righteousness.
v. 19: present your members now to righteousness.
vv. 20–23: the fruit and end of each service: death or eternal life.
kw: Paul calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ” (1:1), using this word. Belonging to God is not a lesser freedom. It is the only service that does not destroy the one who serves.
A soldier's pay, his daily ration money. Sin pays out regularly, and what it pays is death.
A gift of grace, given without being earned. Paul sets it against wages on purpose: death is earned, life is given.
vv: Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!
“By no means” is Paul's strongest denial, literally “may it not be!” Grace is not permission to sin. It is the power not to.
But thanks be to God that you, having once been slaves of sin, have become obedient from the heart to the form of teaching to which you were entrusted,

Paul does not say the teaching was entrusted to them, but that they were entrusted to the teaching, as one hands over a pupil to a master. The POC divides verses 17 and 18 differently, but the sense is the same.
I am speaking in human terms because of your natural limitations.
Paul knows that slavery is a poor picture of life with God, who calls us friends and children. He uses it because it makes the point clear: no one is without a master.
For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
In the POC the first half of this verse closes verse 22. The contrast is complete: wages and gift, sin and God, death and life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the more one does what is good, the more truly one becomes a person who can choose well: there is no true freedom except in the service of what is good and just, and the choice of evil leads to “the slavery of sin” (CCC 1733). It also teaches that death entered the world as a consequence of sin (CCC 1008), and that grace is the help God gives us, undeserved, to respond to his call to become his children and to share eternal life (CCC 1996). Life with God is called slavery only by comparison; in truth it is the life of sons and daughters.

set: Jesus has just told the disciples for the second time that he will be betrayed, killed and after three days rise again, but “they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him” (9:31–32). On the road behind him they talk of something else. In Capernaum, probably in the house of Peter (1:29), he asks them about it. Mark tells the scene in three short movements: a question, a saying, an action.
str: vv. 33–34: the question on arrival, and the disciples' silence.
v. 35: the saying: first by being last, great by being servant.
vv. 36–37: the child in his arms: welcoming the little one is welcoming Christ and the Father.
kw: One who waits at table. In 10:45 Jesus says that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. The Church's word “deacon” comes from it.
In that society a child had no rank and no rights. Jesus takes the one who counts for least and puts him at the centre.
To receive as a guest. To welcome a child “in my name” is to receive Christ himself.
vv: But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another who was the greatest.
Their silence is an answer. They knew their argument would not stand in the light of his question, and on the way to his Passion.
He sat down, called the twelve, and said to them,
A Jewish teacher sat to teach. Jesus gives this lesson with the weight of formal teaching, and to the Twelve, the future leaders of his Church.
“Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”
The chain is the same as in Jesus' words when he sends out the Twelve (Matthew 10:40): the little one, Christ, the Father. Greatness is measured by how we receive those who cannot repay us.
ch: The Catechism teaches that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the kingdom (CCC 526). The Church has tried to keep this saying before her pastors: from the time of St Gregory the Great the Bishop of Rome has called himself “servant of the servants of God”. Every authority in the Church is a service, and every Christian home that welcomes a child, the poor or the unwanted, welcomes Christ.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591). He was the eldest son of a noble Italian family, heir to a title, and he gave his inheritance to his younger brother to enter the Society of Jesus. In 1591, while plague struck Rome, he nursed the sick, caught the disease and died at the age of twenty-three. The Church has given him to young people as their patron. He chose to be last in order to serve, and in him the young can see that Paul's “slavery to God” is a life of joy.
study: Paul says that every person is the slave of the one he obeys. What do my choices of the last week show about whom I am serving?
Who is the “child” in my life, the person who cannot repay me, whom Jesus asks me to welcome in his name?
